In [[computational complexity theory]], the [[complexity class]] ⊕'''P''' (pronounced "parity P") is the class of [[decision problem]]s solvable by a [[nondeterministic Turing machine]] in [[polynomial time]], where the acceptance condition is that the number of accepting computation paths is odd. An example of a ⊕'''P''' problem is "does a given graph have an odd number of [[perfect matching]]s?" The class was defined by [[Christos Papadimitriou|Papadimitriou]] and [[Stathis Zachos|Zachos]] in 1983.<ref>[[Christos Papadimitriou|C. H. Papadimitriou]] and [[Stathis Zachos|S. Zachos]]. [http://portal.acm.org/citation.cfm?id=720053 Two remarks on the power of counting]. In ''Proceedings of the 6th GI Conference in Theoretical Computer Science'', ''Lecture Notes in Computer Science'', volume 145, Springer-Verlag, pp.&nbsp;269–276. 1983.</ref>

An example of a ⊕'''P'''-complete problem (under polynomial-time [[many-one reduction]]s) is ⊕SAT: given a Boolean formula, is the number of its satisfying assignments odd? This follows from the proof of the [[Cook–Levin theorem]] because the reduction used is [[Parsimonious_reduction|parsimonious]].<ref>Abhishek Shetty, Raghav Malhotra, and
Chandan Saha. [https://www.csa.iisc.ac.in/~chandan/courses/complexity15/notes/lec26.pdf Lecture 26] scribe notes from [https://www.csa.iisc.ac.in/~chandan/courses/complexity15/home.html Computational Complexity Theory class], 2015.</ref>

⊕'''P''' is a counting class, and can be seen as finding the least significant bit of the answer to the corresponding '''[[Sharp-P|#P]]''' problem. The problem of finding the most significant bit is in '''[[PP (complexity)|PP]]'''. '''PP''' is believed to be a considerably harder class than ⊕'''P'''; for example, there is a relativized universe (see [[oracle machine]]) where '''P''' = ⊕'''P''' ≠ '''[[NP (complexity)|NP]]''' = '''PP''' = '''[[EXPTIME]]''', as shown by Beigel, [[Harry Buhrman|Buhrman]], and [[Lance Fortnow|Fortnow]] in 1998.<ref>R. Beigel, H. Buhrman, and [[Lance Fortnow|L. Fortnow]]. '''NP''' might not be as easy as detecting unique solutions. In ''Proceedings of [[ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing]] 1998'', pp.&nbsp;203–208. 1998. doi:[https://doi.org/10.1145/276698.276737 10.1145/276698.276737]</ref>

While [[Toda's theorem]] shows that '''P'''<sup>'''PP'''</sup> contains '''[[PH (complexity)|PH]]''', the class '''P'''<sup>⊕'''P'''</sup> is not known to even contain '''NP'''. However, the first part of the proof of Toda's theorem shows that '''[[BPP (complexity)|BPP]]'''<sup>⊕'''P'''</sup> contains '''PH'''. Lance Fortnow has written a concise proof of this theorem.<ref>{{citation
 | first = Lance
 | last = Fortnow
 | title = A simple proof of Toda's theorem
 | journal = Theory of Computing
 | volume = 5
 | year = 2009
 | pages = 135–140
 | doi = 10.4086/toc.2009.v005a007| doi-access = free
 }}</ref>

⊕'''P''' contains the [[graph automorphism problem]], and in fact this problem is [[low (complexity)|low]] for ⊕'''P'''.<ref>{{citation
 | first1 = Johannes
 | last1 = Köbler
 | first2 = Uwe
 | last2 = Schöning
 | first3 = Jacobo
 | last3 = Torán
 | title = Graph isomorphism is low for PP
 | journal = [[Computational Complexity (journal)|Computational Complexity]]
 | volume = 2
 | issue = 4
 | year = 1992
 | pages = 301–330
 | doi = 10.1007/BF01200427}}.</ref> It also trivially contains '''[[UP (complexity)|UP]]''', since all solutions to problems in '''UP''' have either zero or one accepting paths. More generally, ⊕'''P''' is [[low (complexity)|low]] for itself, meaning that such a machine gains no power from being able to solve any ⊕'''P''' problem instantly.

The ⊕ symbol in the name of the class may be a reference to use of the symbol ⊕ in [[Boolean algebra (logic)|Boolean algebra]] to refer the [[exclusive disjunction]] operator. This makes sense because if we consider "accepts" to be 1 and "not accepts" to be 0, the result of the machine is the exclusive disjunction of the results of each computation path.
